source.title: The Lives of Stars
source.attribution: A Reborn guide drawing on NASA Science and the European Space Agency.
source.notes: Written by Reborn in our own words; no text copied. References: NASA Science, Stars, https://science.nasa.gov/universe/stars/; NASA Science, Star Types, https://science.nasa.gov/universe/stars/types/; NASA Science, Sun Facts, https://science.nasa.gov/sun/facts/; ESA/Webb, Pillars of Creation (NIRCam image), https://esawebb.org/images/weic2216a/; NASA Science, Hubble Messier 1 (Crab Nebula), https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/science/explore-the-night-sky/hubble-messier-catalog/messier-1/; NASA Science, Hubble Finds That Betelgeuse's Mysterious Dimming Is Due to a Traumatic Outburst, https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/hubble-finds-that-betelgeuses-mysterious-dimming-is-due-to-a-traumatic-outburst/

cards.title: Every star you see is partway through a life lasting millions to trillions of years
cards.body:
Stars are born, they spend most of their lives quietly burning, and then they die. Some fade gently. Others tear themselves apart in explosions seen across the universe.

We never watch one star live its whole life. A human lifetime is far too short. Instead, astronomers look at thousands of stars caught at different stages, a bit like working out how people age by studying a crowded street of babies, teenagers and grandparents.

From that crowd, a clear story has emerged, checked against physics and measurement. It explains why stars shine, why they come in different colours, and why the atoms in your own body were once inside one. This guide follows that story from cold cloud to final glow.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, pick out three stars of different brightness. Remind yourself that each is at its own point in a life far longer than human history.

quiz.question: How do astronomers learn about the life cycle of stars?
options: By watching a single star from birth to death
By studying many stars caught at different stages of life
By building small stars in laboratories
By reading ancient star charts only
quiz.explanation: Star lives last millions of years or more, so astronomers compare huge numbers of stars at different stages, like piecing together ageing from a crowd of people.

cards.title: Stars are born inside cold, dark clouds of gas and dust
cards.body:
Between the stars drift vast clouds called nebulae, made mostly of hydrogen with a sprinkling of dust. Some stretch for hundreds of light-years. Many are extremely cold, only a few degrees above absolute zero.

When part of a cloud gets a nudge, perhaps from a nearby exploding star or a passing shock wave, gravity can take over. A dense clump starts to collapse, pulling in more material. As it shrinks it spins faster and heats up, often flattening into a disc around a growing centre.

That glowing centre is a protostar, a star not yet switched on. The leftover disc can go on to form planets. Our own Sun and planets formed this way about 4.6 billion years ago. Telescopes that see infrared light, such as Webb, can peer through the dust and watch this happening today.
cards.apply_it: Find a picture of the Orion Nebula, a nearby stellar nursery. On a dark winter night you can spot it as a faint smudge in Orion's sword.

quiz.question: What usually triggers a stellar nursery cloud to start forming stars?
options: The cloud getting very hot
Gravity pulling a dense clump together, sometimes after a nudge
Light from the Moon
The cloud running out of hydrogen
quiz.explanation: A disturbance can compress part of a cloud, and gravity then pulls the dense clump inward until it becomes a protostar.

cards.title: The Pillars of Creation are star factories light-years tall
cards.body:
In 1995 the Hubble Space Telescope photographed three dark towers of gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula, about 6,500 light-years away. The image became one of the most famous in astronomy, and the towers were nicknamed the Pillars of Creation.

They are enormous. The tallest pillar is roughly four light-years long, which is about the distance from the Sun to the nearest other star. Inside them, dense knots of gas are collapsing into new stars.

The pillars are also being slowly destroyed. Fierce light from hot young stars nearby is boiling away their outer layers. In 2022 the James Webb Space Telescope looked again in infrared light and revealed many newborn stars glowing inside and around them, like embers in smoke.
cards.apply_it: Look up the Hubble and Webb images of the Pillars of Creation side by side. Notice how infrared light reveals stars the visible-light picture hides.

quiz.question: Roughly how tall is the tallest of the Pillars of Creation?
options: About 4 kilometres
About the width of the Solar System
About four light-years
About 4,000 light-years
quiz.explanation: The tallest pillar stretches roughly four light-years, about the distance from the Sun to the nearest neighbouring star.

cards.title: A star switches on when its core reaches about 10 million degrees
cards.body:
A collapsing clump of gas grows hotter as gravity squeezes it. For a long time it glows only from that squeezing, not from nuclear reactions.

The real turning point comes when the core reaches roughly 10 million degrees Celsius. At that temperature, hydrogen nuclei are moving fast enough to collide and fuse. The energy released pushes outward and balances the inward pull of gravity. The collapse stops, and a true star is born.

That balance is the secret of a star's long, steady life: gravity crushing in, fusion energy pushing out, each keeping the other in check. If a clump has too little mass, about less than 8% of the Sun's, it never gets hot enough. It becomes a brown dwarf, a failed star that slowly cools.
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel stuck in a tug-of-war between two pressures, remember that every star lives inside one. Balance, not stillness, is what keeps it shining.

quiz.question: What happens to an object that has too little mass to start hydrogen fusion?
options: It becomes a neutron star
It becomes a brown dwarf
It explodes as a supernova
It turns into a planet like Earth
quiz.explanation: Below roughly 8% of the Sun's mass, the core never gets hot enough to fuse hydrogen steadily, so the object becomes a brown dwarf, sometimes called a failed star.

cards.title: The Sun turns about four million tonnes of itself into energy every second
cards.body:
Deep in the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei are fused into helium. It takes four hydrogen nuclei, through a chain of steps, to make one helium nucleus.

Here is the twist: the helium weighs slightly less than the hydrogen that made it. That missing mass has become energy, following Einstein's famous equation, E equals m c squared. Because the speed of light squared is a huge number, a tiny amount of mass gives a vast amount of energy.

Every second, the Sun fuses roughly 600 million tonnes of hydrogen, and about four million tonnes of mass vanish as energy. That sounds alarming, but the Sun is so massive that it has lost only a tiny fraction of itself in 4.6 billion years. We know this works because the same physics is measured in laboratories and detected in particles called neutrinos streaming from the Sun's core.
cards.apply_it: Step outside in daylight and feel the warmth on your skin. Reflect that it began as mass disappearing in the Sun's core.

quiz.question: Where does the energy released by fusion in the Sun come from?
options: Burning hydrogen with oxygen, like a fire
A small amount of mass being converted into energy
Electricity from the Sun's magnetic field
Heat left over from the Big Bang
quiz.explanation: The helium produced weighs slightly less than the hydrogen that went in. That lost mass becomes energy, as described by E = mc².

cards.title: The Sun is an ordinary star with a core of about 15 million degrees
cards.body:
Our Sun is a fairly average star, which is exactly why it is so useful to study. It is a ball of hot plasma about 1.4 million kilometres across, wide enough to line up roughly 109 Earths side by side. It holds about 99.8% of all the mass in our Solar System.

At its core the temperature is around 15 million degrees Celsius, and the pressure is crushing. The visible surface is far cooler, at about 5,500 degrees. Strangely, the thin outer atmosphere, the corona, reaches over a million degrees, and why it is so hot is still being investigated by spacecraft such as Parker Solar Probe.

The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old, roughly halfway through its life as a hydrogen-burning star.
cards.apply_it: Never look directly at the Sun. Instead, use a pinhole in card to project its image onto paper and see the disc of an ordinary star.

quiz.question: About how many Earths could line up across the Sun's diameter?
options: About 10
About 109
About 1,000
About 1 million
quiz.explanation: The Sun is about 1.4 million kilometres across, which is roughly 109 times Earth's diameter. About a million Earths would fit inside it by volume.

cards.title: Sunlight on your face may have spent many thousands of years escaping the Sun
cards.body:
Light reaches us from the Sun's surface in about 8 minutes and 20 seconds. The journey from the core to that surface is far slower.

The inside of the Sun is so dense that energy cannot travel straight out. In the inner zone, light is absorbed and re-emitted again and again, each time heading off in a random direction, like a person trying to leave a packed stadium by bumping from one stranger to the next.

Estimates of how long this random walk takes vary, from tens of thousands of years to around 170,000 years. After that, the energy is carried up through the outer layers by churning, boiling gas, much like a pan of soup. So the warmth you feel today began its journey long before the first farms and cities on Earth.
cards.apply_it: Sit in the sunshine for one minute. Picture the energy reaching you as having left the Sun's core before human history was written.

quiz.question: Why does energy take so long to get from the Sun's core to its surface?
options: The Sun is spinning too fast
Light is absorbed and re-emitted countless times in random directions
Light travels more slowly in a vacuum
The core only releases energy once a year
quiz.explanation: The dense interior makes light bounce in a random walk, so its energy takes many thousands of years to work its way out before the final 8-minute trip to Earth.

cards.title: The Sun breathes out a wind that blows past every planet
cards.body:
The Sun is not only giving off light. It also flings out a constant stream of charged particles called the solar wind. It typically travels at around 400 kilometres per second, and faster streams move at about twice that.

This wind carries the Sun's magnetic field with it and blows out past all the planets, carving a vast bubble in space called the heliosphere. Earth's magnetic field shields us from most of it, steering some particles toward the poles, where they help create the aurora.

We know where the bubble ends because we have been there. In 2012, Voyager 1 crossed its edge and entered interstellar space, the first human-made object to do so. Voyager 2 followed in 2018. Both are still sending back data.
cards.apply_it: If you ever see an aurora, or a photo of one, remember it is partly the Sun's wind meeting Earth's magnetic shield.

quiz.question: What happened to Voyager 1 in 2012?
options: It landed on the Sun
It crossed the edge of the Sun's bubble into interstellar space
It reached the nearest star
It was destroyed by a solar flare
quiz.explanation: In 2012 Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the edge of the bubble blown by the solar wind, and became the first spacecraft in interstellar space.

cards.title: A solar flare can release more energy in minutes than humanity uses in many years
cards.body:
The Sun's magnetic field gets twisted as different parts of the Sun spin at different speeds. Sometimes the tangled field snaps and reconnects, releasing a sudden burst of radiation called a solar flare. The biggest flares release energy equivalent to billions of large nuclear bombs in a matter of minutes.

Flares often come with coronal mass ejections, giant clouds of charged gas hurled into space. When one hits Earth it can trigger brilliant auroras far from the poles.

It can also cause trouble. In 1859, during what is called the Carrington Event, telegraph systems sparked and failed. A storm that strong today could disrupt satellites and power grids, which is why agencies such as NASA and ESA now watch the Sun constantly and issue space weather forecasts.
cards.apply_it: Look up today's space weather forecast online. Check whether auroras might be visible from where you live.

quiz.question: What was notable about the Carrington Event of 1859?
options: It was the first eclipse ever recorded
A huge solar storm disrupted telegraph systems
The Sun briefly stopped shining
A comet hit the Sun
quiz.explanation: In 1859 a powerful solar storm produced auroras far from the poles and made telegraph systems spark and fail.

cards.title: A star's colour is its thermometer, and blue means hottest
cards.body:
Look closely at the night sky and you will notice that stars are not all white. Some glow faintly orange or red, others blue-white.

That colour tells us the temperature of the star's surface. It works like heating a metal poker: it glows red first, then orange, then white as it gets hotter. The coolest stars, at around 3,000 degrees Celsius, look red. The Sun, at about 5,500 degrees, gives out light that is actually close to white. The hottest stars blaze blue at over 30,000 degrees.

This is a surprise for many people: on Earth's everyday scale, red means hot and blue means cold. In the stars it is the opposite. Astronomers measure this precisely by splitting starlight into a spectrum.
cards.apply_it: On a clear night, compare reddish Betelgeuse with blue-white Rigel in Orion. You are looking at a difference of thousands of degrees.

quiz.question: What does a blue star tell you compared with a red star?
options: It is cooler
It is hotter
It is closer to Earth
It is older
quiz.explanation: Star colour depends on surface temperature. Blue stars are the hottest and red stars are the coolest.

cards.title: Red dwarfs will shine for trillions of years, and not one has died yet
cards.body:
The most common stars in our galaxy are small, cool ones called red dwarfs. They make up roughly three-quarters of all stars in the Milky Way, yet not one is visible to the naked eye. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, is a red dwarf.

Red dwarfs burn their fuel extremely slowly. Their insides churn, stirring fresh hydrogen into the core so very little is wasted. As a result, models predict they can last for trillions of years.

The universe is only about 13.8 billion years old. That means every red dwarf that has ever formed is still shining. When the bigger, brighter stars are long gone, these small, dim stars will still be glowing, the last lights of the cosmos.
cards.apply_it: Reflect: the slow and steady stars outlast the brilliant ones by a factor of hundreds. Where in your life might patience beat brilliance?

quiz.question: Why has no red dwarf star ever died?
options: They are protected by dark matter
Their lifespans are far longer than the current age of the universe
They are not real stars
They constantly absorb other stars
quiz.explanation: Red dwarfs can live for trillions of years, while the universe is only about 13.8 billion years old, so none has had time to run out of fuel.

cards.title: The bigger the star, the shorter its life
cards.body:
You might expect a star with more fuel to last longer. The reverse is true.

A heavier star has stronger gravity squeezing its core, which makes the core hotter and fusion much faster. It burns through its hydrogen at a furious rate. The Sun will spend about 10 billion years in its stable phase. A star 20 times the Sun's mass may last only around 10 million years, a blink in cosmic terms.

Mass is the single most important fact about a star. It sets the star's brightness, colour, lifespan and the way it will die. Small stars like the Sun end gently as white dwarfs. Stars more than about eight times the Sun's mass end in supernova explosions, leaving behind neutron stars or black holes.
cards.apply_it: Think about something you do in short, intense bursts and something you do slowly. Which lasts longer for you?

quiz.question: Why do massive stars have shorter lives than smaller ones?
options: They are born with less fuel
Their stronger gravity makes their cores hotter, so they burn fuel much faster
They are hit by more comets
They are further from the galaxy's centre
quiz.explanation: Greater mass means more gravitational squeezing, a hotter core and much faster fusion, so a massive star uses up its fuel quickly.

cards.title: Some stars are so large they would swallow the orbit of Mars
cards.body:
The Sun is big, but it is far from the biggest. The largest known stars, called red supergiants and hypergiants, are more than a thousand times wider than the Sun. Placed where the Sun is, the edge of such a star would reach beyond Mars and, for the largest, towards Jupiter.

Size and mass are not the same. These giants are swollen and puffy, with outer layers far thinner than the air around you. The most massive star known, R136a1 in a neighbouring galaxy, is roughly 200 times the Sun's mass and millions of times brighter, though it is much more compact than the supergiants.

Measuring the size of a distant star is difficult, and estimates for the very largest often change. What is certain is that the range of stars is enormous.
cards.apply_it: Picture the Sun as a grape. On that scale, the largest known stars would be bigger than a house.

quiz.question: What is true about the largest known stars?
options: They are also the densest stars
They can be more than a thousand times wider than the Sun
They are all red dwarfs
They are found only in our Solar System
quiz.explanation: Red supergiants and hypergiants can be over a thousand times wider than the Sun, though their outer layers are extremely thin.

cards.title: In about five billion years, the Sun will swell into a red giant
cards.body:
When the Sun runs low on hydrogen in its core, the core will shrink and heat up while the outer layers balloon outwards and cool. The Sun will become a red giant, perhaps hundreds of times wider than it is today.

Mercury and Venus will almost certainly be swallowed. Whether Earth is engulfed is still uncertain, because the Sun will also lose a great deal of mass, which lets the planets drift outward. Either way, Earth will be scorched long before that. The Sun is slowly brightening, and in roughly a billion years it will probably be too hot for oceans to survive.

We can be confident about the broad story because we see many red giants in the sky today, including Arcturus and Aldebaran, at exactly this stage.
cards.apply_it: Find Arcturus, a bright orange star, in spring or summer skies. You are looking at a preview of the Sun's future.

quiz.question: Which planets are expected to be swallowed when the Sun becomes a red giant?
options: Jupiter and Saturn
Mercury and Venus, with Earth's fate uncertain
Only Mars
None, the Sun will shrink instead
quiz.explanation: Mercury and Venus will almost certainly be engulfed. Earth's fate is uncertain because the Sun will lose mass and the planets' orbits will widen.

cards.title: Planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets
cards.body:
As a Sun-like star nears its end, it gently puffs off its outer layers into space. The exposed hot core lights up those expanding shells of gas, which glow in brilliant colours and shapes: rings, hourglasses, butterflies and spirals.

These are called planetary nebulae, a name that is a historical accident. In the 1780s, William Herschel thought they looked like the round discs of planets through his telescope. The name stuck, even though they are actually dying stars.

They are also short-lived. A planetary nebula fades in only tens of thousands of years, a moment in a star's life of billions. The Ring Nebula and the Helix Nebula are famous examples, and our Sun is expected to make one of its own.
cards.apply_it: Look up an image of the Helix Nebula, sometimes called the Eye of God. You are seeing the final breath of a star like our Sun.

quiz.question: What is a planetary nebula?
options: A cloud where planets are forming
Glowing gas shed by a dying Sun-like star
A planet that has exploded
A galaxy full of planets
quiz.explanation: It is the expanding outer layers of a dying Sun-like star, lit up by the hot core left behind. The name comes from its planet-like look in early telescopes.

cards.title: A white dwarf packs the Sun's mass into a ball the size of Earth
cards.body:
Once a Sun-like star has shed its outer layers, all that remains is its core, a white dwarf. It no longer has fusion, so it simply glows from stored heat.

A white dwarf can hold around the mass of the Sun in a sphere roughly the size of Earth. Its matter is so tightly packed that a teaspoonful would weigh several tonnes, about as much as an elephant. What holds it up is not heat but a quantum effect: electrons resist being squeezed into the same state.

The nearest example is Sirius B, a faint companion to Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, about 8.6 light-years away. About 97% of stars in our galaxy, including the Sun, are expected to end their lives this way.
cards.apply_it: Find Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. Hidden in its glare is a white dwarf, the future of our Sun.

quiz.question: Roughly how big is a white dwarf?
options: About the size of a city
About the size of Earth
About the size of the Sun
About the size of the Solar System
quiz.explanation: A white dwarf packs roughly a Sun's worth of mass into a ball about the size of Earth.

cards.title: Black dwarfs may one day exist, but the universe is too young for any yet
cards.body:
White dwarfs cool down slowly over time, like embers after a fire. Theory predicts that given enough time, one would cool so far that it no longer glows at all. Such a cold, dark remnant is called a black dwarf.

This is a prediction, not something anyone has seen. Calculations suggest cooling that far would take vastly longer than the universe's current age of 13.8 billion years, perhaps a million billion years or more. So, if the theory is right, not one black dwarf exists anywhere yet.

The idea rests on well-tested physics of how white dwarfs lose heat, and astronomers check those cooling models by measuring the oldest, faintest white dwarfs in our galaxy. Those observations support the theory, but the black dwarf itself remains a forecast for an extremely distant future.
cards.apply_it: Reflect: some things are predicted so far ahead that no one could ever see them happen. How does it feel to think on that timescale?

quiz.question: Why have no black dwarfs been observed?
options: They are too small to see
The universe is not yet old enough for any white dwarf to cool that far
They only form inside black holes
They were destroyed in the Big Bang
quiz.explanation: Theory says a white dwarf would need far longer than 13.8 billion years to cool into a black dwarf, so none should exist yet.

cards.title: A dying giant star can collapse in under a second and outshine its galaxy
cards.body:
A star more than about eight times the Sun's mass fuses heavier and heavier elements in its core, ending with iron. Iron is a dead end: fusing it absorbs energy rather than releasing it. With nothing left to hold it up, the core collapses in a fraction of a second.

The infalling matter rebounds and a colossal shock blasts the star apart. This is a core-collapse supernova. For weeks, a single exploding star can shine as brightly as billions of Suns.

We know a lot of this from direct evidence. In 1987 a supernova lit up in a nearby galaxy, the Large Magellanic Cloud, and detectors on Earth caught a burst of neutrinos from its collapsing core hours before the light was seen. What remains is a neutron star, or for the heaviest stars, a black hole.
cards.apply_it: Next time something falls apart suddenly after a long build-up, remember the giant star: its collapse also scatters the materials for something new.

quiz.question: Why does iron in a massive star's core lead to its collapse?
options: Iron is radioactive
Fusing iron absorbs energy rather than releasing it
Iron is magnetic
Iron makes the star spin faster
quiz.explanation: Fusing iron does not release energy, so the core loses the outward push holding it up and collapses almost instantly.

cards.title: In 1054, a new star appeared in daylight, and its wreckage is still expanding
cards.body:
In the year 1054, astronomers in China recorded a 'guest star' so bright that it was visible in daylight for weeks. It then faded from view.

Centuries later, telescopes pointed at the same spot found the Crab Nebula, a tangled cloud of glowing gas about 6,500 light-years away and roughly 10 light-years across. Measuring how fast it is expanding and running the clock backwards points to an explosion around the 11th century, matching the old records.

At the heart of the Crab sits the collapsed core of the star: a neutron star spinning about 30 times every second, still powering the nebula's glow. It is one of the best-studied objects in the sky, a link between medieval sky-watchers and modern space telescopes.
cards.apply_it: With binoculars or a small telescope on a dark winter night, look near the tip of Taurus's horn. The faint smudge there is the Crab Nebula.

quiz.question: What lies at the centre of the Crab Nebula?
options: A planet like Jupiter
A rapidly spinning neutron star
A young Sun-like star
Nothing at all
quiz.explanation: The Crab Nebula's core holds a neutron star, the collapsed remnant of the star that exploded in 1054, spinning about 30 times a second.

cards.title: A teaspoon of neutron star would weigh billions of tonnes
cards.body:
When the core of a massive star collapses, it can be crushed into a neutron star. These objects typically hold more mass than the Sun, yet they are only about 20 kilometres across, roughly the size of a city.

The squeeze is so extreme that atoms are crushed and electrons and protons merge into neutrons. The result is matter packed about as densely as an atomic nucleus. A single teaspoonful would weigh billions of tonnes, more than all the people on Earth put together.

Gravity at the surface is so strong that a mountain could rise no more than a few millimetres high. Light leaving a neutron star is bent by its gravity enough that you could see part of its far side. All of this is consistent with measurements of real neutron stars in binary systems.
cards.apply_it: Imagine a city-sized ball weighing more than the Sun. Hold a teaspoon and try to picture it outweighing every human alive.

quiz.question: About how wide is a typical neutron star?
options: About 20 kilometres
About the width of Earth
About the width of the Sun
About one light-year
quiz.explanation: Neutron stars hold more than the Sun's mass in a sphere only about 20 kilometres across, roughly the size of a city.

cards.title: Some dead stars spin hundreds of times a second, ticking like cosmic clocks
cards.body:
In 1967, Jocelyn Bell Burnell, then a graduate student in Cambridge, noticed a strange signal in radio telescope data: a pulse repeating every 1.3 seconds with remarkable regularity. Half-jokingly, the team labelled it LGM-1, for 'little green men'.

It turned out to be a pulsar, a spinning neutron star. Beams of radiation stream from its magnetic poles. As the star turns, the beams sweep past Earth like a lighthouse, so we see a pulse each rotation.

The fastest known pulsar spins about 716 times per second. A body more massive than the Sun, rotating faster than a kitchen blender. Some pulsars keep time almost as well as atomic clocks, and astronomers now use networks of them to detect ripples in spacetime called gravitational waves.
cards.apply_it: Tap your finger once per second. Now imagine a star heavier than the Sun turning hundreds of times between each tap.

quiz.question: Why do we see pulsars as regular pulses?
options: They switch on and off
Their beams sweep past Earth as they spin, like a lighthouse
Clouds pass in front of them
They are orbited by flashing planets
quiz.explanation: A pulsar beams radiation from its magnetic poles. As it rotates, the beams sweep across Earth once per turn, producing regular pulses.

cards.title: Magnetars have the strongest magnetic fields known in the universe
cards.body:
A magnetar is a neutron star with an extraordinary magnetic field, up to about a thousand trillion times stronger than Earth's. Even from halfway to the Moon, it could wipe the data from every credit card on Earth.

These fields are so intense they can crack the star's crust, unleashing sudden flares of X-rays and gamma rays. On 27 December 2004, a giant flare from a magnetar about 50,000 light-years away, on the far side of our galaxy, released more energy in a fraction of a second than the Sun gives out in many thousands of years. It was strong enough to measurably disturb Earth's upper atmosphere.

Only a few dozen magnetars are known. Their fields are thought to fade within about ten thousand years, so we catch them only while young.
cards.apply_it: Hold a fridge magnet. Then picture a field so strong it would distort atoms themselves, and remember it exists in a star the size of a city.

quiz.question: What made the magnetar flare of December 2004 so remarkable?
options: It was visible to the naked eye for a year
It disturbed Earth's upper atmosphere from about 50,000 light-years away
It created a new planet
It destroyed a nearby galaxy
quiz.explanation: The giant flare came from across the galaxy, about 50,000 light-years away, yet it still measurably affected Earth's upper atmosphere.

cards.title: Colliding neutron stars forge gold, and in 2017 we watched it happen
cards.body:
On 17 August 2017, gravitational wave detectors in the United States and Europe picked up ripples in spacetime from two neutron stars spiralling together and merging, about 130 million light-years away.

Within seconds a burst of gamma rays was seen, and within hours telescopes worldwide found a new point of light in a distant galaxy. This was a kilonova, the glowing debris of the collision. Its light carried the fingerprints of freshly made heavy elements, including signs of the kind of matter that forms gold and platinum.

It was the first time a single cosmic event was observed in both gravitational waves and light. It confirmed that neutron star mergers are real factories for many of the heaviest elements on the periodic table.
cards.apply_it: If you own anything made of gold, look at it for a moment. Some of its atoms were likely forged in a collision of dead stars.

quiz.question: What did the 2017 neutron star merger confirm?
options: That the Sun will become a black hole
That such mergers produce heavy elements like gold
That neutron stars do not exist
That gravitational waves travel slower than light
quiz.explanation: The kilonova's light showed freshly made heavy elements, confirming neutron star mergers as factories for elements such as gold and platinum.

cards.title: Nobody knows exactly where most of the universe's gold came from
cards.body:
Neutron star mergers definitely make gold. What is not settled is whether they made most of it.

The puzzle is about timing and quantity. Neutron star mergers can take a very long time to happen after the stars form, yet some very old stars already contain surprising amounts of heavy elements. That suggests other factories may have been at work early in cosmic history.

Candidates include rare kinds of supernovae, such as the collapse of rapidly spinning, highly magnetic massive stars, and giant flares from magnetars. Each idea has supporters, and the true answer may be a mix. Astronomers are testing them by catching more mergers with gravitational wave detectors, studying the chemistry of ancient stars, and refining computer simulations. For now, the full origin story of gold remains open.
cards.apply_it: Think of a question in your own field where the main answer is known but the details are still being argued. What would settle it?

quiz.question: Why do scientists doubt that neutron star mergers made all of the universe's gold?
options: Mergers have never been observed
Some very old stars already contain heavy elements, possibly earlier than mergers could supply
Gold is only made on Earth
Gold cannot be made by stars
quiz.explanation: Mergers can take a long time to happen, but some ancient stars already hold heavy elements, hinting that other sources were also involved.

cards.title: The oxygen you breathe and the calcium in your bones were made inside stars
cards.body:
The Big Bang produced almost only hydrogen and helium, with a trace of lithium. Nearly every heavier element came later, made by stars.

Carbon, nitrogen and oxygen were built by fusion in stellar cores and released when stars shed their layers or exploded. Much of the iron in your blood was made in exploding stars. Some of the heaviest elements came from collisions of neutron stars.

Add it up and about 90% of your body's mass is made of atoms that were once inside stars. Most of the rest is hydrogen dating from the Big Bang itself. The old saying that we are made of star stuff is not poetry, it is chemistry. Astronomers know this by matching the elements seen in stars, nebulae and supernova remains with what nuclear physics predicts.
cards.apply_it: Take a deep breath. Reflect that the oxygen filling your lungs was forged in a star that died before the Sun was born.

quiz.question: Which elements did the Big Bang mainly produce?
options: Carbon and oxygen
Iron and gold
Hydrogen and helium
Calcium and nitrogen
quiz.explanation: The Big Bang made almost only hydrogen and helium, plus a little lithium. Heavier elements were later forged in stars and stellar explosions.

cards.title: Betelgeuse will explode one day, but nobody knows when
cards.body:
Betelgeuse, the reddish shoulder of Orion, is a red supergiant hundreds of times wider than the Sun, roughly 550 to 700 light-years away. Distance estimates vary. It is near the end of its life and is expected to explode as a supernova.

In late 2019 and early 2020 it dimmed dramatically, sparking excitement. Observations from Hubble and other telescopes showed the cause: the star had thrown off a huge cloud of material that cooled into dust and blocked some of its light. It was not about to explode.

When will it go? Nobody knows. The best estimates say sometime within roughly the next 100,000 years. When it does, it may shine as brightly as a half Moon for weeks. It is far too distant to harm us.
cards.apply_it: In winter, find Orion and look at its top-left shoulder. That orange star could explode at any time in the next 100,000 years.

quiz.question: What caused Betelgeuse's 'Great Dimming' in 2019 to 2020?
options: It was about to explode
A cloud of dust from material the star threw off
The Moon passed in front of it
It ran out of hydrogen overnight
quiz.explanation: Telescope observations showed Betelgeuse had ejected a large cloud of material that cooled into dust and temporarily hid part of its light.

cards.title: Some stars near us are almost as old as the universe itself
cards.body:
Not far from the Sun, about 190 light-years away, is a faint star called HD 140283, sometimes nicknamed the Methuselah star. Recent estimates put its age at around 12 to 14 billion years, with real uncertainty, making it one of the oldest stars known.

How can we tell? Old stars formed when the universe had few heavy elements, so their light shows very little iron and other metals. Astronomers also compare a star's brightness and temperature with models of how stars age.

These ancient stars are living fossils. They formed less than two billion years after the Big Bang and are still shining today. Many old stars orbit in the halo around our galaxy and in dense balls called globular clusters, survivors from the Milky Way's early days.
cards.apply_it: Look up the globular cluster M13 in Hercules. With binoculars it appears as a fuzzy ball, made of stars older than most of the galaxy.

quiz.question: How can astronomers tell that a star is very old?
options: It is always the brightest star nearby
Its light shows very few heavy elements such as iron
It is always red
It moves faster than light
quiz.explanation: The earliest stars formed before many heavy elements existed, so a very low level of iron and other metals is a sign of great age.

cards.title: No one has yet confirmed seeing the very first stars
cards.body:
The first generation of stars formed from pure hydrogen and helium, a few hundred million years after the Big Bang. Theory suggests they may have been huge, perhaps hundreds of times the Sun's mass, short-lived and very hot. They would have made the first heavy elements and helped light up the young universe.

But nobody has confirmed seeing one. They are far too distant and faint to spot individually, and none should survive today because massive stars die quickly.

The James Webb Space Telescope is hunting for their combined glow in the most distant galaxies, and has reported possible hints, though none is yet confirmed. Astronomers are also searching the Milky Way for very old stars carrying the chemical fingerprints those first stars left behind. What they were really like remains one of astronomy's open questions.
cards.apply_it: Reflect: our universe once had no stars at all. Imagine the first one switching on in total darkness.

quiz.question: Why can we not see a first-generation star in our galaxy today?
options: They were all invisible
They were probably massive and short-lived, so they died long ago
They are hidden behind the Sun
They never existed
quiz.explanation: The first stars were probably very massive, and massive stars burn out quickly, so none would still be shining today.

cards.title: The Sun is a loner, but many stars have partners
cards.body:
Our Sun travels through space alone. Many stars do not. Roughly half of Sun-like stars have one or more companions, orbiting each other in binary or multiple star systems. Smaller red dwarfs are more often single.

Our nearest neighbour is a family of three: Alpha Centauri A and B orbit each other closely, with Proxima Centauri circling much further out.

Binaries are hugely useful. By timing their orbits, astronomers can weigh stars directly, which is how we know many stellar masses. Some pairs line up so that one passes in front of the other. Algol, in Perseus, dims noticeably every few days for exactly this reason. When stars orbit very close, one can pull gas from the other, which can lead to dramatic outbursts and even some kinds of supernovae.
cards.apply_it: Look at Mizar, the middle star in the handle of the Plough or Big Dipper. Good eyesight shows a faint companion, Alcor, beside it.

quiz.question: Why are binary stars especially useful to astronomers?
options: They are always the brightest stars
Their orbits let us measure the stars' masses directly
They never change brightness
They are closer than the Sun
quiz.explanation: Timing how two stars orbit each other allows astronomers to calculate their masses, one of the most important facts about any star.

cards.title: Stars twinkle because of Earth's air, not because of the stars
cards.body:
Stars do not flicker in space. The twinkle is added in the last few kilometres of their journey, as their light passes through Earth's atmosphere.

Air is constantly moving, with pockets of warmer and cooler air bending light by slightly different amounts. Stars are so far away that each is effectively a single point of light, so these small shifts make it jump and change brightness, and sometimes flash colours, especially near the horizon.

Planets are much closer and appear as tiny discs rather than points. The wobbles average out across the disc, so planets usually shine more steadily. This is a handy way to tell them apart. It is also one reason telescopes are placed on high mountains or in space, and why big observatories use adaptive optics to cancel out the twinkle.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, compare a star low on the horizon with one high overhead. Notice which twinkles more, and spot a planet by its steady light.

quiz.question: Why do planets usually twinkle less than stars?
options: Planets make their own light
Planets appear as tiny discs, so atmospheric wobbles average out
Planets are outside Earth's atmosphere
Planets are hotter than stars
quiz.explanation: Because planets are close enough to show as tiny discs rather than points, the shimmering of the air averages out and their light looks steadier.

cards.title: You are seeing stars as they were, but almost all of them are still there
cards.body:
Starlight takes time to reach us. Light from Sirius left about 8.6 years ago. Light from some bright stars in Orion left centuries ago. Looking up is always looking into the past.

This leads to a popular claim: that many of the stars you see are already dead. For the naked-eye sky, this is almost never true. Most stars you can see without a telescope are within a few thousand light-years, so their light is at most a few thousand years old. Stars live for millions to billions of years, so the chance that any particular one has died in that short gap is tiny.

A few exceptions are possible. Betelgeuse, for example, could in principle have exploded already. But nearly every star in your night sky is still shining right now.
cards.apply_it: Pick a star tonight and think about what was happening on Earth when its light set out.

quiz.question: Is it true that many of the stars we see with the naked eye are already dead?
options: Yes, most of them are dead
No, their light is relatively recent compared with star lifetimes, so nearly all are still alive
Yes, all stars we see are dead
No, because starlight arrives instantly
quiz.explanation: Naked-eye stars are mostly within a few thousand light-years, while stars live millions to billions of years, so almost all are still shining.

cards.title: The stars made us, and one day our atoms may help make new stars
cards.body:
Follow the story of stars and it loops back to you. A cold cloud collapses, a star ignites, it shines for millions or billions of years, and it dies, scattering new elements into space. Those elements gather in the next cloud, and the cycle begins again.

Our Sun is at least a second- or third-generation star, built partly from the remains of earlier ones. The Earth, the oceans and your own body came from that recycled material.

Billions of years from now, when the Sun sheds its outer layers, atoms that were once part of our world may drift into space and join a future nursery. Nothing in this story is wasted. You are part of a cycle that has been running for more than 13 billion years.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, look at the darkest patch of sky you can find. Reflect that you are made of atoms that once shone there, and may again.

quiz.question: What happens to many of the elements a star makes when it dies?
options: They vanish completely
They are scattered into space and can become part of new stars and planets
They fall into the nearest black hole
They stay locked inside the dead star forever
quiz.explanation: Dying stars shed or blast their elements into space, where they mix into new clouds that form the next generations of stars and planets.
